final_proof:
Write \(n1_R\) for the additive integer multiple of \(1_R\), and put
\[
T=\{n1_R:n\in\mathbb Z\}.
\]
For all \(m,n\in\mathbb Z\), distributivity gives
\[
(m1_R)+(n1_R)=(m+n)1_R,
\qquad -(n1_R)=(-n)1_R,
\]
and
\[
(m1_R)(n1_R)=mn(1_R1_R)=(mn)1_R.
\]
The multiplicative identity follows first for nonnegative integers by repeated distributivity; the cases involving negative integers follow by taking additive inverses. Consequently \(T\) is a subring of \(R\) containing \(1_R\). Conversely, every subring of \(R\) containing \(1_R\) is closed under addition and additive inverses, so it contains \(n1_R\) for every \(n\in\mathbb Z\). Hence \(T\) is precisely the subring \(S\) generated by \(1_R\).

The same identities show that
\[
g(m+n)=g(m)+g(n),\qquad g(mn)=g(m)g(n),
\]
and \(g(1)=1_R\). Thus \(g\) is a ring homomorphism with image \(T=S\), and is therefore an epimorphism onto \(S\).

Now suppose that \(R\) has no proper zero divisors, so that \(ab=0_R\) implies \(a=0_R\) or \(b=0_R\), and use the standard convention that a ring with unity is nontrivial, i.e. \(1_R\ne0_R\). Let \(f:\mathbb Z\to R\) be any ring homomorphism, not necessarily assumed to preserve unity, and set \(e=f(1)\). Additivity implies
\[
f(n)=ne\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z),
\]
while multiplicativity gives \(e^2=f(1)^2=f(1)=e\). Hence
\[
e(e-1_R)=0_R.
\]
If \(f\) is nonzero, then \(e\ne0_R\), since otherwise \(f(n)=ne=0_R\) for every \(n\). The absence of proper zero divisors therefore forces \(e-1_R=0_R\). Thus \(e=1_R\), and
\[
f(n)=n1_R=g(n)
\]
for every integer \(n\). Therefore \(g\) is the unique nonzero homomorphism from \(\mathbb Z\) into \(R\).

It remains to determine its kernel, still under the no-proper-zero-divisors hypothesis. Every ideal of \(\mathbb Z\) has the form \(d\mathbb Z=(d)\) for a unique integer \(d\ge0\), so write
\[
\ker g=d\mathbb Z.
\]
If \(d=0\), the kernel is the zero ideal. Since \(g\) is already surjective onto \(S\), it is then an isomorphism \(\mathbb Z\cong S\).

Suppose instead that \(d>0\). We cannot have \(d=1\), because that would put \(1\) in \(\ker g\), contrary to \(g(1)=1_R\ne0_R\). If \(d\) were composite, write \(d=ab\) with \(1<a<d\) and \(1<b<d\). Then
\[
0_R=g(d)=g(a)g(b).
\]
Since \(R\) has no proper zero divisors, either \(g(a)=0_R\) or \(g(b)=0_R\). Thus either \(a\in d\mathbb Z\) or \(b\in d\mathbb Z\), which is impossible because \(0<a,b<d\). Therefore \(d\) is prime. Writing \(p=d\), we obtain
\[
\ker g=p\mathbb Z=(p).
\]
By the first isomorphism theorem,
\[
S=\operatorname{im}g\cong \mathbb Z/\ker g
 =\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z_p,
\]
which is a field because \(p\) is prime. These are exactly the two asserted alternatives, with \((0)\) denoting the zero ideal of \(\mathbb Z\).
